items.en: Cultivating and Realizing the Sixteen Special Excellences: Knowing the Breath
items.zh: 十六特勝 · 明修證 · 知息入出、長短、遍身

zh: 第三、明修證者，所以心名修證者，即是作心修習。心未相應證者，即是任運開發，心得相應。既有三師制立觀法不同，今亦修有證之異，但前師云：「於欲界、未到地及初禪中，約四念處明十六特勝。」觀法大意亦不異如前說六妙門中觀法，而非無小小不同。而名目有異，善尋配當，其義可解，此則不煩別說修證也。今正明後師竪對三界明真特勝。既上來未說此觀慧方法，今當出修證之相。
en: Third, clarifying their cultivation and realization: as for why this is spoken of as "cultivating and realizing": cultivating refers precisely to the mind's own deliberate cultivation and practice, while the mind has not yet come to correspondence; realizing refers to its opening forth spontaneously, the mind coming to correspond with it. Since there are, as already given, differing schemes for establishing the contemplation-method among these three masters, cultivation and realization likewise differ accordingly here as well — though the first master says: "Within the desire realm, the 'not-yet-arrived' state, and the first dhyāna, the sixteen special excellences are clarified with reference to the four foundations of mindfulness." The general sense of this contemplation-method does not differ from the contemplation-method already given within the six wondrous gates, though it is not entirely without small differences — the terms used differ, but, properly sought out and matched accordingly, the sense may be readily understood, and so this need not be separately explained here in terms of cultivation and realization.

Here, then, the second master's own scheme is directly clarified: the true special excellences, corresponding vertically through the three realms. Since the method of this contemplative wisdom has not yet been explained above, its mark of cultivation and realization shall now be set forth.

zh: 竪明修十六特勝者：一、知息入；二、知息出。此對代數息也。調息方法，事事如前數息中說。行者既調息綿綿，一心依隨於息，息若入時，知從鼻端入至臍；若出時，知從臍出至鼻。如是一心照息，依隨不亂，爾時知息麁細之相。麁者，知風喘氣為麁；細者，知息相為細。若入息麁時，即調之令細，是名知麁細相。譬如守門之人，知門人出入，亦知好人、惡人，知好則進，知惡則遮。復次，知麁細者，入息則麁，出息則細。何故爾？入氣利急故相麁，出息澁遲故細。復次，知輕重，知入息時輕，出息時重。何以故？入息既在身內，即令體輕；出息時，身無風氣，則覺身重。復次，知澁滑：入息時滑，出息時澁。何以故？息從外來，風氣利故，則滑；從內出吹，內滓穢，塞諸毛孔，則澁。復次，知冷暖：知入息時冷，知出息時暖。何以故？息從外來，冷氣而入，故冷；息從內出，吹內熱氣而出，故暖。復次，知久近：入息時近，出息時久。何以故？息入既利，則易盡，故近；息出澁，則難盡，故久。復須覺知因出入息故，則有一切眾苦煩惱，生死往來，輪轉不息，心知驚畏。行者隨息之時，知息有如是等法相非一，故云知息入出也。
en: Explaining the vertical cultivation of the sixteen special excellences: first, knowing the breath entering; second, knowing the breath leaving. These correspond to, and take the place of, counting the breath. The method for regulating the breath is, in every particular, exactly as already given within counting the breath. The practitioner, the breath now regulated and continuous, fixes the mind single-mindedly on following the breath: when it enters, one knows it as entering from the tip of the nose all the way to the navel; when it leaves, one knows it as leaving from the navel all the way to the nose. Illuminating the breath single-mindedly in this way, following it without disorder, one becomes aware, at this point, of the coarse and fine marks of the breath. As for the coarse: knowing the wind and panting breath as coarse. As for the fine: knowing the breath's own mark as fine. If the in-breath is coarse, one regulates it, making it fine — this is named knowing the marks of coarse and fine.

It is like a gatekeeper, aware of everyone entering and leaving through the gate, likewise able to recognize the good person from the bad — recognizing the good, allowing them to pass; recognizing the bad, barring their way. Furthermore, as for knowing coarse and fine: the in-breath is coarse, and the out-breath is fine. Why is this? The in-breath's own energy is sharp and urgent, and so its mark is coarse; the out-breath is sluggish and slow, and so is fine. Furthermore, knowing light and heavy: knowing the in-breath as light, and the out-breath as heavy. Why is this? The in-breath, now present within the body, causes the body to feel light; at the moment of the out-breath, the body has no wind-energy present within it, and so is felt as heavy. Furthermore, knowing rough and smooth: the in-breath is smooth, and the out-breath is rough. Why is this? The breath comes from outside, its wind-energy sharp, and so is smooth; going out from within, blowing out the body's own inward filth, obstructing the various pores, it is thus rough. Furthermore, knowing cold and warm: knowing the in-breath as cold, and the out-breath as warm. Why is this? The breath comes from outside, cold air entering, and so is cold; the breath goes out from within, blowing out the body's own inward heat, and so is warm. Furthermore, knowing long-lasting and brief: the in-breath is brief, and the out-breath is long-lasting. Why is this? The in-breath, being sharp, is quickly exhausted, and so is brief; the out-breath, being rough, is not easily exhausted, and so is long-lasting.

One must further become aware that, because of this very in-breath and out-breath, every kind of suffering and affliction exists, coming and going through birth-and-death, turning without cease — the mind knowing this, and growing alarmed and fearful. The practitioner, at the time of following the breath, comes to know that the breath carries such marks and dharmas as these, not of one kind only — hence this is called knowing the breath entering and leaving.

zh: 問：何故以此代數息？答：若是數息，直闇心數，無有觀行，修證時多生愛、見、慢等諸煩惱病也。愛者，愛著此數息；見者，謂見我能數；慢者，謂我能數，以此慢他。今以隨代數者，隨息之時，即覺知此息無常，命依於息，以息為命，一息不還，即便無命。既覺息無常，知身命危脆。知息無常，即不生愛；知息非我，即不生見；悟無常，即不生慢。此則從初方便已能破諸結使，不同數息。復次，行者一心依息，令心不散，得入禪定，故名亦愛；覺悟無常，故名亦策；與定相應，名亦有漏；觀行不著，名亦無漏。復次，若數息時冥闇心而數，既無照了，後證定時，則心無所見。今隨息者既明心照息，後證定時，則心眼開明，見身三十六物，破愛、見、慢。此即是特勝勝於數息也。
en: Question: why is this used in place of counting the breath? Answer: were one simply counting the breath, this counting is done with a mind still in the dark, without any contemplative practice present at all, and so, at the time of cultivation and realization, tends to give rise to such afflictive ailments as craving, wrong views, and pride. Craving: growing attached to this very counting of the breath. Views: taking the view that "I" am the one able to count. Pride: taking pride that "I" am able to count, and, through this, feeling superior to others.

Here, following the breath is used in place of counting it: at the time of following the breath, one becomes aware directly that this very breath is impermanent — life itself depends upon the breath, the breath being taken as one's very life — and, should a single breath fail to return, life itself would be gone at once. Becoming aware of the breath's own impermanence, one thereby knows the body and its life to be perilous and frail. Knowing the breath as impermanent, craving no longer arises; knowing the breath as not-self, wrong views no longer arise; and awakening to impermanence, pride no longer arises. This, then, is already able, from the very first expedient means onward, to break through the fetters — unlike counting the breath alone.

Furthermore: the practitioner, fixing the mind single-mindedly on the breath, keeping the mind from scattering, is able to enter dhyāna-concentration through this — hence it, too, may be named a form of attachment; becoming aware of impermanence — hence it, too, may be named a spur; corresponding with concentration — hence it, too, is contaminated; and its contemplative practice not clinging to anything — hence it, too, is uncontaminated. Furthermore: were one counting the breath with a mind still in the dark, there being no illumination present at all, then, later, at the time concentration is actually realized, the mind would have nothing to see. Here, however, one who follows the breath already illuminates the mind, contemplating the breath directly, so that, later, at the time concentration is actually realized, the mind's own eye opens into clarity, seeing the body's thirty-six substances, breaking through craving, views, and pride. This is precisely how the special excellences surpass mere counting of the breath.

The first two items already demonstrate the whole method's guiding logic: they occupy the exact functional slot of counting the breath, but replace bare mechanical repetition with an awareness of the breath's own impermanence built in from the very first step — the same craving/views/pride triad the six wondrous gates' own counting-stage was vulnerable to is here preempted before it can take hold, rather than corrected for later. The gatekeeper simile — recognizing good visitors from bad, admitting one and barring the other — gives a concrete image for what "knowing" the breath's marks actually means in practice: not passive awareness but active, discriminating attention.

items.en: Breath's Length and Shortness, and Pervading the Body
items.zh: 十六特勝 · 明修證 · 知息長短、遍身
parent: Cultivating and Realizing the Sixteen Special Excellences: Knowing the Breath
十六特勝 · 明修證 · 知息入出、長短、遍身

zh: 三、知息長短者，此對欲界定。若證欲界定時，宜是定明淨都不覺知息中相貌。今此中初得定時，即覺息中長短之相。云何為覺？若心定時，覺入息長，出息短。何以故？心既靜住於內，息隨心入故，入則知長。既心不緣外，故出則知短。復次，覺息長，則心細；覺息短，則心麁。何以故？心細則息細，息細則入從鼻至臍，微緩而長，出息從臍至鼻亦爾。心麁則息麁，息麁則入從鼻至臍，急疾短，出從臍至鼻亦爾。
en: Third, knowing the breath's length and shortness: this corresponds to desire-realm concentration. When desire-realm concentration is realized, the concentration itself is properly bright and pure, without any perception at all of the breath's own mark. Here, however, at the very moment this concentration is first attained, one becomes aware directly of the mark of the breath's own length and shortness.

How is this perceived? When the mind is concentrated, one perceives the in-breath as long and the out-breath as short. Why is this? The mind, now stilled and abiding within, the breath follows the mind inward, and so the in-breath is known as long; and, the mind no longer taking any external object, the out-breath is thus known as short. Furthermore: perceiving the breath as long corresponds to a fine mind; perceiving the breath as short corresponds to a coarse mind. Why is this? A fine mind produces a fine breath, and a fine breath, entering from the nose to the navel, is faint, gentle, and long, the out-breath from navel to nose being the same. A coarse mind produces a coarse breath, and a coarse breath, entering from the nose to the navel, is urgent and short, the out-breath from navel to nose being the same.

zh: 復次，息短故，覺心細；息長故，覺心麁。何以故？如心既轉靜，出息從臍至胸即盡，入息從鼻至咽間即知盡。此則心靜故，覺息短。覺長故心麁者，如行者心麁故，覺息從臍至鼻，從鼻至臍，道里長遠，此則心麁故，覺息長。復次，短中覺長則定細，長中知短則是麁。何故爾？如息從鼻至胸則盡，此行處雖短，而時若大，久久方至，臍。此則行處短而時節長也。若就此而論，短中覺長則定細。覺長中而短是麁者，如心麁故，息從鼻至臍，道里極長，而時節短，欻然之間，即出至鼻。何以故？心麁氣息行疾故。此雖長而短，然此息短則是心麁也，故云短中長而細，長中短而麁也。如此覺長短時節，知無常由心，生滅不定故。今息長短相貌非一，得此定時，覺悟無常，轉更分明。證欲界定，故名亦愛；觀行覺無常，故名亦策。此略說第三、知息長短，破欲界定也。
en: Furthermore: because the breath is short, the mind is perceived as fine; because the breath is long, the mind is perceived as coarse. Why is this? As the mind grows ever more still, the out-breath, from navel to chest, is exhausted at once, and the in-breath, from nose to throat, is likewise known to be exhausted at once — this, then, is the mind's own stillness causing the breath to be perceived as short. As for perceiving it as long, corresponding to a coarse mind: the practitioner's mind being coarse, the breath is perceived as traveling the long distance from navel to nose, and nose to navel — this, then, is the mind's own coarseness causing the breath to be perceived as long.

Furthermore: perceiving length within shortness corresponds to a fine concentration; perceiving shortness within length is instead coarse. Why is this? As when the breath, from nose to chest, is exhausted — this course, though short in distance, nonetheless takes a comparatively long time, only gradually reaching the navel; this, then, is a short course but a long duration. Discussed on this basis, perceiving length within shortness corresponds to a fine concentration. As for perceiving shortness within length being coarse: as when, the mind being coarse, the breath's course, from nose to navel, is an exceedingly long distance, and yet its duration is short, passing through to the nose again in a sudden instant. Why is this? Because a coarse mind causes the breath's own movement to be swift. Though this course is long, its duration is short — and this very shortness of duration is itself what marks the mind as coarse. Hence it is said: shortness containing length corresponds to fineness, and length containing shortness corresponds to coarseness.

Perceiving length and shortness of duration in this way, one comes to know that impermanence arises from the mind itself, its arising and ceasing never fixed. Now, the mark of the breath's own length and shortness being manifold, at the very moment this concentration is attained, awakening to impermanence grows all the more distinct. Realizing desire-realm concentration — hence it, too, may be named a form of attachment; its contemplative practice perceiving impermanence — hence it, too, may be named a spur. This, in brief, describes the third item, knowing the breath's length and shortness, breaking through desire-realm concentration.

zh: 第四、知息遍身者，對未到地定。若根本未到地，直覺身相泯然如虛空，爾時實有身息，但以眼不開故，不覺不見。今特勝中發未到地時，亦泯然入定，即覺漸漸有身如雲影，覺出入息遍身毛孔，爾時亦知息長短相等。見息入無積聚，出無分散，無常生滅，覺身空假不實，亦知生滅剎那不住，三事和合，故有定生。三事既空，則定無所依，知空亦空，於定中不著，即破根本未到地，愛、策之義已在其中。
en: Fourth, knowing the breath pervading the whole body: this corresponds to the "not-yet-arrived" concentration. Within the root "not-yet-arrived" state, one perceives only that the mark of the body has grown indistinct, as though it were empty space — at that point, the body and breath are, in truth, still genuinely present, only that, the eye not yet open, they are neither perceived nor seen.

Here, within the special excellences, when the "not-yet-arrived" state is brought forth, one likewise enters concentration indistinctly, but then becomes aware, gradually, of a body present once again, like a cloud or shadow, perceiving the in-breath and out-breath pervading every pore of the body — and, at this point, one also knows the mark of the breath's own length and shortness alike. Seeing the in-breath as gathering nowhere, and the out-breath as scattering nowhere, impermanent, arising and ceasing, one perceives the body as empty, provisional, and unreal, and also knows that its arising and ceasing never remain still for a single instant, these three matters combining together to produce concentration. These three matters being themselves empty, concentration thereby has nothing at all to depend upon — and, knowing even this very emptiness as itself empty, one no longer clings to anything within concentration at all. This, then, breaks through the root "not-yet-arrived" state, the sense of both attachment and spur already contained within it.

zh: 問：《摩訶衍》中及諸經多說觀息入出，何以故言知息入出？答：此說知為觀，而觀法實未具足，故今說為知。《大品．廣乘品》中明十六特勝相，皆言知息入出長短，以是文為證說知，則不乖文義。觀慧在下當說。
en: Question: the Mahāyāna treatise and the various sūtras, for the most part, speak of "observing" the breath entering and leaving — why, then, is it spoken of here as "knowing" the breath entering and leaving? Answer: this speaks of "knowing" as itself a form of observing, though the method of observation is not yet fully complete — hence it is spoken of here as "knowing" instead. The Larger Sūtra's own chapter on the vast vehicle, in clarifying the mark of the sixteen special excellences, likewise speaks throughout of "knowing" the breath entering, leaving, long, and short — taking this very text as evidence, speaking of "knowing" here does not run contrary to the text's own sense. Contemplative wisdom itself will be discussed below.

The recurring short-within-long / long-within-short paradox (a short physical course taking a long time, a long course passing in an instant) is a genuinely careful phenomenological observation: length and shortness turn out not to be single, simple properties of the breath at all, but at least two independent measures — spatial distance and felt duration — that can point in opposite directions at once, and the treatise uses exactly this mismatch as the empirical hook for realizing that "impermanence arises from the mind itself." The "knowing versus observing" clarification is a small but careful piece of terminological housekeeping, anticipating a reader who might otherwise think the treatise's own vocabulary contradicts the sūtras it is built on.

quiz.q: Why does the text not separately explain cultivation under the first master's mindfulness scheme?
options: the method does not differ from the six gates; only the names differ, and matching them makes it clear
quiz.why: Its method does not differ from that of the six gates apart from small points and names, so it need not be explained separately; the text turns to the later master's vertical scheme.

quiz.q: In the vertical scheme, what do knowing the breath entering and leaving replace, and what path does the breath take?
options: they replace counting; entering from the nose-tip to the navel, leaving from the navel to the nose
they replace following; nose to lungs
they replace stilling; mouth to heart
quiz.why: They take the place of counting; one knows the breath entering from the nose-tip to the navel and leaving from the navel to the nose.

quiz.q: What simile illustrates knowing the coarse and fine breath?
options: a gatekeeper who knows who comes and goes, admitting the good and barring the bad
quiz.why: Like a gatekeeper aware of everyone coming and going, recognizing the good and admitting them, recognizing the bad and barring them.

quiz.q: Which description of the in-breath and out-breath matches the text?
options: in-breath coarse, light, smooth, cold, brief; out-breath fine, heavy, rough, warm, long-lasting
quiz.why: The in-breath is coarse, light, smooth, cold, and brief; the out-breath fine, heavy, rough, warm, and long-lasting.

quiz.q: Why does the body feel light on the in-breath and heavy on the out-breath?
options: the in-breath within the body makes it light; with no wind-energy on the out-breath, it feels heavy
quiz.why: The in-breath, present within the body, makes it feel light; on the out-breath there is no wind-energy within, so it feels heavy.

quiz.q: Why does mere counting tend to give rise to craving, views, and pride, and what are they?
options: counting in the dark without contemplation; craving for counting, the view that "I" count, and pride over others
quiz.why: Counting is done in the dark without contemplation, so craving (attachment to counting), views (that "I" count), and pride (feeling superior for counting) arise.

quiz.q: How does following the breath in place of counting break craving, views, and pride?
options: knowing the breath impermanent, craving does not arise; not-self, views do not arise; awakening to impermanence, pride does not arise
quiz.why: Life depends on the breath, and one breath not returning ends it; knowing this, craving, views, and pride do not arise, so even the first expedient breaks the fetters.

quiz.q: In what respects is following the breath called attachment, spur, contaminated, and uncontaminated?
options: entering concentration: attachment; awakening to impermanence: spur; corresponding with concentration: contaminated; contemplation without clinging: uncontaminated
quiz.why: Entering concentration by the breath is attachment; awakening to impermanence is a spur; corresponding with concentration is contaminated; contemplation without clinging is uncontaminated.

quiz.q: How does awareness of the breath differ between the root desire-realm concentration and the special excellences?
options: the root concentration perceives no mark of the breath; in the excellences one perceives its length and shortness at once
quiz.why: In the root desire-realm concentration one perceives no mark of the breath; in the special excellences, on first attaining it, one perceives its length and shortness.

quiz.q: Why, when the mind is concentrated, is the in-breath perceived as long and the out-breath short?
options: the mind abides within and the breath follows it in, so the in-breath is long; not taking outer objects, the out-breath is short
quiz.why: The mind abides within and the breath follows it inward, so the in-breath is long; not taking outer objects, the out-breath is short.

quiz.q: How is "length within shortness is fine; shortness within length is coarse" to be understood?
options: a short course taking a long time marks fine concentration; a long course passing in an instant marks a coarse mind
quiz.why: A short course taking a long time marks fine concentration; a long course passing in an instant marks a coarse mind, since a coarse mind makes the breath swift. Thus impermanence arises from the mind.

quiz.q: Knowing the breath pervading the body corresponds to the not-yet-arrived state. How does it differ from the root not-yet-arrived state?
options: the root state sees the thirty-six substances
the body vanishes in the excellences
the root state feels the body vanish like space, unseen because the eye is closed; in the excellences one gradually sees the body like a cloud-shadow, the breath through every pore
quiz.why: In the root state the body seems to vanish like space, though body and breath are present but unseen; in the excellences one gradually perceives a body like a cloud or shadow, the breath through every pore.

quiz.q: The treatise and sūtras mostly say "observing" the breath. Why does this text say "knowing"?
options: knowing is a form of observing not yet complete; the Larger Sūtra's chapter also says "knowing"
quiz.why: "Knowing" is a form of observing whose method is not yet complete; the Larger Sūtra's chapter also uses "knowing," so it does not contradict the texts.
